summary: Gives guidelines for end-to-end quality of service in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 domain whose access network uses IEEE 802.11. It describes mapping the QoS negotiated between MAG and LMA, per RFC 7222, to Wi-Fi mechanisms.

eli5.summary: A guide to translating priority rules between two systems, so a video call on Wi-Fi keeps its fast lane while moving around a network.

questions: proxy mobile ipv6 quality of service
how does wifi qos map to pmipv6
subtitle: How Wi-Fi admission control requests line up with Proxy Mobile IPv6 QoS signaling.

tldr.problem: Quality of service in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network is negotiated between the MAG and LMA, while Wi-Fi sets up QoS between the station and the access point with different procedures and parameters. Nothing tied the two together.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps IEEE 802.11 and WMM-AC procedures (ADDTS, DELTS, TSPEC, TCLAS) to PMIPv6 QoS messages and options, and gives tables mapping flows, DSCP and access categories, and bandwidth parameters.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational companion to RFC 7222 for building end-to-end QoS over Wi-Fi in a PMIPv6 domain. Network-initiated reservations remain hard because 802.11 gives the access point no standard way to ask the client.

today: RFC 7561 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is written as a companion to RFC 7222.

sections.title: Two QoS Worlds to Join
sections.content:
RFC 7222 describes an access-network-independent way to negotiate Quality of Service (QoS) for Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) sessions. IEEE 802.11, Wi-Fi Multimedia (WMM) and WMM Admission Control (WMM-AC) provide QoS between a Wi-Fi station and an Access Point (AP). This RFC shows how to combine them, so end-to-end QoS works when the access network is Wi-Fi.

The modeled network has a Mobile Node (MN), an AP combined with a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) located at the AP or Wireless LAN Controller, and a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA). Protocols between the AP and MAG are out of scope.

Two mismatches must be handled. First, PMIPv6 QoS can be triggered by the LMA or MAG, but 802.11 QoS setup is always triggered by the MN. Second, there is no systematic parameter mapping: for example, Allocation and Retention Priority in PMIPv6 QoS has no 802.11 equivalent. The main focus is interworking between WMM-AC signaling and PMIPv6 QoS signaling.
sections.eli5: Wi-Fi and the mobile network each have their own way to ask for a fast lane. This document explains how to pass the request from one to the other.

sections.title: IEEE 802.11 QoS in Brief
sections.content:
IEEE 802.11 gives prioritized access to different traffic through Enhanced Distributed Channel Access (EDCA). There are four access categories, in decreasing priority: Voice, Video, Best-Effort and Background (AC_VO, AC_VI, AC_BE, AC_BK). Higher categories use smaller Contention Window and Arbitration Inter-Frame Space values.

WMM is a Wi-Fi Alliance certification of a subset of these features. It maps the eight IEEE 802.1P priorities onto the four categories. WMM does not support the TCLAS element, which identifies an IP flow, and that affects the mapping.

A non-AP station can ask the AP to reserve QoS for an access category by sending an ADDTS request, and the AP admits or denies it based on resources. The AP may require admission control for a category, and WMM-AC is the certification for that. All of this signaling starts at the station.
sections.eli5: Wi-Fi has four lanes: voice, video, normal and background. A device can ask the access point to reserve a place in a fast lane, and the access point says yes or no.

sections.title: Mapping the Procedures
sections.content:
When the MN starts the request, it sends an ADDTS request with a TSPEC and, optionally, a TCLAS. The MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) with QoS options and Operational Code ALLOCATE, and the LMA answers with a Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA). The AP then returns an ADDTS response with the authorized QoS. Without TCLAS, the flow details may need to come from an Application Layer Gateway or Deep Packet Inspection, which adds complexity; if none is derived, the reservation applies to all flows of the MN.

If the LMA offers downgraded QoS, the AP answers with REJECTED_WITH_SUGGESTED_CHANGES, so the MN may retry lower. If the LMA cannot meet the request (status code 179, CANNOT_MEET_QOS_SERVICE_REQUEST), the result is TCLAS_RESOURCES_EXHAUSTED. Neither removes the session itself.

Releases work in both directions. The MN sends DELTS and the MAG sends a PBU with DE-ALLOCATE. Alternatively the LMA sends an Update Notification (UPN) with DE-ALLOCATE, the MAG replies with an Update Notification Acknowledgement (UPA), and the AP sends DELTS to the MN.
sections.eli5: When your device asks for a fast lane, the access point checks with the network's boss and passes the answer back. When the call ends, either side can say 'you can give the lane back now'.

sections.title: Network-Initiated Requests
sections.content:
When the LMA starts a QoS request, there is no standard way in 802.11 for the AP to ask the MN to reserve anything. So the PMIPv6 request and any Wi-Fi request are handled asynchronously. If the MAG gets a UPN for which the MN has made no request, it may, with the AP, prepare a policy that can grant a later request from the MN. If the MN then asks for a rate the earlier PMIPv6 provisioning supports, the AP can accept. If there is a mismatch, either the MAG renegotiates for more resources or the AP rejects the request.

IEEE 802.11aa has an ADDTS Reserve Request that lets the AP ask a client to reserve QoS, but it requires a stream identifier and the specification does not say how the AP gets one. The RFC says a new higher-layer protocol would be needed, or the identifier would have to become optional. Appendix A shows a sequence that would apply if these issues were resolved.
sections.eli5: Wi-Fi has no standard way for the access point to tap a device and say 'reserve a lane'. So the network gets ready in advance and waits for the device to ask.

sections.title: Mapping the Parameters
sections.content:
Flows. A TCLAS element with Classifier 1 (TCP/UDP parameters) maps one-to-one to the PMIPv6 Traffic Selector (IP flow), and the TCLAS DSCP maps to the Traffic Class. Without TCLAS, the bandwidth applies to all flows of the MN, or the flow is derived out-of-band by watching signaling such as SIP.

QoS class. A table maps QoS Class Identifier (QCI) and DSCP to 802.1D user priority and access category. For example, QCI 1 to 3 use DSCP EF and AC_VO, and QCI 9 uses best effort and AC_BK. Reservations use only AC_VO and AC_VI; AC_BE and AC_BK should not be used. Without TCLAS, there can be only one reservation per access category.

Bandwidth. TSPEC Mean Data Rate should map to the Guaranteed bit rate parameters, and Peak Data Rate should map to the Aggregate-Max bit rate parameters, in both directions. If the MN asks for more than PMIPv6 QoS authorized, the AP should deny the request and may suggest acceptable values.
sections.eli5: Each Wi-Fi setting has a matching setting on the network side: the kind of traffic, the lane, and how fast it may go. This is the matching list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC maps parameters between two signaling systems, so the security of both and of the nodes doing the mapping must be considered. IEEE 802.11 can secure the management frames used for ADDTS and DELTS. The PMIPv6 specification (RFC 5213) recommends IPsec and IKEv2 to secure its messages. The QoS mappings themselves do not introduce additional security concerns.
sections.eli5: Both sides already have ways to keep messages safe. This translation does not add new risks, but the translator itself should be protected.

messages.note: The MN asks for QoS for a flow.

messages.note: TSPEC parameters are mapped to PMIPv6 parameters.

messages.note: The LMA returns the authorized QoS.
